claim: PNKP knockout U2OS cells (PNKP−/− cells) were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 Nickase (D10A) targeting exon 4 of the PNKP coding region.
source: To confirm that this phenotype is observed in human cells, we initially generated PNKP knockout U2OS cells (PNKP−/− cells) using CRISPR/Cas9 Nickase (D10A) targeting exon 4 of the PNKP coding region (Chiang et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used to generate PNKP knockout cells, supported by citation to Chiang et al., 2016.

claim: Two PNKP knockout clones (C1 and C2) showed complete loss of PNKP as confirmed by western blot analysis with both N-terminus and C-terminus PNKP-recognized antibodies and DNA sequencing.
source: We obtained two clones (C1 and C2) that showed complete loss of PNKP, as confirmed by western blot analysis with both N-terminus and C-terminus PNKP-recognized antibodies and DNA sequencing (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in western blots and DNA sequencing results presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: PNKP−/− cells showed a delay in diminishing the phosphorylation of histone H2AX and KAP1 after IR-induced DNA damage.
source: PNKP−/− cells showed a delay in diminishing the phosphorylation of histone H2AX and KAP1, markers of DSBs, after IR-induced DNA damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing delayed reduction of phosphorylation markers in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PNKP−/− cells showed increased sensitivity to IR exposure, suggesting a defect in DSB repair ability.
source: PNKP−/− cells also showed increased sensitivity to IR exposure, suggesting a defect in DSB repair ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data showing increased sensitivity to IR in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PNKP−/− cells displayed a significantly increased level of native BrdU signals and hyper-sensitivity upon SSB induction by hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
source: The cells displayed a significantly increased level of native BrdU signals and hyper-sensitivity upon SSB induction by hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), indicating that the loss of PNKP leads to reduced ability of SSB repair in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU incorporation assay data and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: PNKP−/− cells showed increased sensitivity to the inhibition of DNA replication by hydroxyurea (HU) treatment.
source: Furthermore, PNKP−/− cells showed increased sensitivity to the inhibition of DNA replication by hydroxyurea (HU) treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data showing increased sensitivity to HU in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: PNKP−/− cells grow slower than WT cells.
source: During the course of our experiments, we observed that PNKP−/− cells grow slower than WT cells, consistent with our previous study in mice (Figure 1B; Shimada et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth curve data in Figure 1B and citation to previous study in mice.

claim: PNKP−/− cells accumulate in the S phase.
source: The analysis revealed an accumulation of PNKP−/− cells in the S phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing cell cycle distribution in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: PNKP−/− clones exhibited significantly higher levels of ADP-ribosylation compared to WT cells.
source: Our two PNKP−/− clones exhibited significantly higher levels of ADP-ribosylation, a marker of ssDNA gaps/breaks, compared to WT cells, indicating that PNKP−/− cells face a pronounced amount of endogenously induced ssDNA gaps/breaks.
evidence: The claim is supported by PAN ADP-ribosylation assay data showing increased ADP-ribosylation in PNKP−/− cells.

claim: HU and EME treatment rescued the increased ADP-ribose intensity in PNKP−/− cells.
source: Although PNKP−/− cells showed high levels of ADP-ribose intensity spontaneously, HU and EME treatment rescued the increased ADP-ribose intensity in PNKP−/− cells, albeit higher, yet statistically non-significant, extent than WT cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data with HU and EME treatments.

claim: Loss of PNKP leads to an accumulation of ssDNA gap structures during DNA replication.
source: This suggests that loss of PNKP leads to an accumulation of ssDNA gap structures during DNA replication.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of ADP-ribose intensity by HU and EME treatment, which inhibit DNA replication.

claim: PNKP−/− cells exhibited faster progression of DNA replication fork than WT cells.
source: Despite the slower cell growth, PNKP−/− cells exhibited faster progression of DNA replication fork than WT cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data showing increased tract length in Figure 1G.

claim: PNKP−/− cells exhibited significantly shortened DNA fibers upon S1 nuclease-mediated DNA digestion.
source: In addition, PNKP−/− cells exhibited significantly shortened DNA fibers upon S1 nuclease-mediated DNA digestion, unlike U2OS WT cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by S1 DNA fiber assay data showing shortened DNA fibers after S1 nuclease treatment.

claim: Loss of PNKP results in the accumulation of ssDNA gaps on nascent replicated DNA.
source: This observation suggests that the loss of PNKP results in the accumulation of ssDNA gaps on nascent replicated DNA, leading to improper cell proliferation due to high levels of endogenous DNA damage (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the S1 nuclease digestion data and supported by a model in Figure 1H.

claim: FEN1i treatment induced increased CldU tract length in U2OS WT cells.
source: Indeed, FEN1i treatment induced increased CldU tract length, whereas HU treatment led to stalled forks, consistent with previous studies (Thakar et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data and citation to previous study.

claim: Double treatment of FEN1i and PARPi in U2OS WT cells, followed by S1 nuclease treatment, showed significantly lower CldU/IdU ratio, indicating extensive DNA fiber digestion by S1 nuclease.
source: Double treatment of FEN1i and PARPi in U2OS WT cells, followed by S1 nuclease treatment, showed significantly lower CldU/IdU ratio, indicating extensive DNA fiber digestion by S1 nuclease (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by S1 DNA fiber assay data in Figure 2C showing reduced CldU/IdU ratio.

claim: Both FEN1-dependent canonical OFs maturation and PARP-dependent ssDNA gap-filling pathway are coordinately required to prevent the emergence of ssDNA gaps during DNA replication.
source: Although single treatment with either FEN1i or PARPi in U2OS WT cells, followed by S1 nuclease treatment, led to DNA fiber digestion, the extent was limited compared to the double treatment (Figure 2C, D), indicating that both pathways: FEN1-dependent canonical OFs maturation and PARP-dependent ssDNA gap-filling pathway, are coordinately required to prevent the emergence of ssDNA gaps during DNA replication, consistent with previous studies (Vaitsiankova et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by S1 DNA fiber assay data comparing single and double inhibitor treatments, and citation to previous study.

claim: PNKP−/− cells with S1 nuclease treatment showed extensive DNA fiber digestion even without FEN1i and PARP1i treatments.
source: On the other hand, PNKP−/− cells with S1 nuclease treatment showed extensive DNA fiber digestion even without FEN1i and PARP1i treatments, and this was not further increased by FEN1i and PARPi treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by S1 DNA fiber assay data showing extensive digestion in PNKP−/− cells without inhibitor treatment.

claim: PNKP is involved in both FEN1-dependent canonical OFs maturation and PARP-dependent ssDNA gap-filling pathway.
source: These results suggest that PNKP itself is involved in both pathways mentioned above (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PNKP−/− cells show extensive DNA fiber digestion without inhibitor treatment, suggesting involvement in both pathways.

claim: D2 mutant-expressing cells showed slower proliferation than cells expressing WT PNKP and other mutants.
source: D2 mutant-expressing cells showed slower proliferation than cells expressing WT PNKP and other mutants, although D3 and D4 exhibited mildly slower cell proliferation (WT vs. D3: p = 0.1737; WT vs. D4: p = 0.4523).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth rate data comparing different PNKP deletion mutants.

claim: D3, D4 as well as D2 mutant-expressing cells showed increased tract lengths compared to WT and D1 mutant-expressing cells.
source: Furthermore, D3, D4 as well as D2 mutant-expressing cells showed increased tract lengths compared to WT and D1 mutant-expressing cells, indicating that in addition to the enzymatic activity of PNKP, the linker region also plays a crucial role in proper fork progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data comparing different PNKP deletion mutants.

claim: The linker region of PNKP plays a crucial role in proper fork progression.
source: Furthermore, D3, D4 as well as D2 mutant-expressing cells showed increased tract lengths compared to WT and D1 mutant-expressing cells, indicating that in addition to the enzymatic activity of PNKP, the linker region also plays a crucial role in proper fork progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that D2 (linker deletion) mutant shows slower proliferation and increased tract length.

claim: Five potential phosphorylation sites were identified in the PNKP linker region: serine 114, threonine118, threonine 122, serine 126, and serine 143.
source: Using PhosphoSitePlus, we identified five potential phosphorylation sites: serine 114, threonine118, threonine 122, serine 126, and serine 143 (Figure 3D; Hornbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis using PhosphoSitePlus database and citation.

claim: Amino acids S114, T118, and S143 are highly conserved among mammalian species.
source: Amino acids S114, T118, and S143 are highly conserved among mammalian species.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: S114 is phosphorylated by ATM and S126 by ATM and DNA-PKcs.
source: S114 and S126 form a typical SQ/TQ motif, with S114 being phosphorylated by ATM and S126 by ATM and DNA-PKcs (Segal-Raz et al., 2011; Zolner et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T118 is predicted to be a CDK phosphorylation substrate motif (S/TP).
source: T118, T122, and S143 are novel phosphorylation sites, with T118 predicted to be a CDK phosphorylation substrate motif (S/TP).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis identifying the S/TP motif.

claim: T118A mutant-expressing cells exhibited a marked delay in cell growth.
source: T118A mutant-expressing cells exhibited a marked delay in cell growth, which was not observed in S114A, although T122A (p = 0.0258), S126A (p = 0.0523), and S143A (p = 0.4402) showed slight delays.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth rate data comparing different PNKP point mutants.

claim: The linker region of PNKP, especially the phosphorylation of PNKP on T118, is required for proper cell proliferation.
source: These results suggest that the linker region of PNKP, especially the phosphorylation of PNKP on T118, is required for proper cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that T118A mutant shows marked delay in cell growth.

claim: pT118-PNKP was detected in asynchronized cells but increased particularly in the S phase, similar to Cyclin A2 expression levels.
source: pT118-PNKP was detected in asynchronized cells but increased particularly in the S phase, similar to Cyclin A2 expression levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from synchronized cells showing increased pT118-PNKP in S phase.

claim: T118 phosphorylation was very weak during mitosis.
source: However, the reduction of pT118, possibly due to dephosphorylation of T118, was not as robust as the reduction in Cyclin A2 expression levels at the 12 hr time point. This effect was very weak during mitosis, suggesting that T118 phosphorylation plays a specific role in the S phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from synchronized cells showing weak pT118-PNKP during mitosis.

claim: CDK1/Cyclin A2 and CDK2/Cyclin A2 markedly phosphorylated PNKP at T118.
source: CDK1/Cyclin A2 and CDK2/Cyclin A2 markedly phosphorylated PNKP, whereas CDK4/Cyclin D1 and CDK2/Cyclin E1 phosphorylated PNKP to a lesser extent, suggesting that CDK1/CyclinA2 and CDK2/CyclinA2 complexes are potential kinases of PNKP T118.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing phosphorylation of PNKP by CDK/Cyclin complexes.

claim: Overexpression of both CDK2/Cyclin A2 and CDK1/Cyclin A2 showed an increased phosphorylation level at T118.
source: Overexpression of both CDK2/Cyclin A2 and CDK1/Cyclin A2 showed an increased phosphorylation level at T118, supporting that these complexes are potential kinases of PNKP T118.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from cells co-expressing CDK/Cyclin complexes and PNKP.

claim: PNKP T118A mutant showed a reduced amount of protein interaction with both CDK1 and CDK2.
source: PNKP T118A mutant showed a reduced amount of protein interaction with both CDK1 and CDK2, with CDK2 appearing as a stronger binding partner of PNKP.
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-pulldown assay data showing reduced interaction between T118A mutant and CDKs.

claim: CDK1/2, especially CDK2, are the kinases of T118 on PNKP.
source: These results indicate that CDK1/2, especially CDK2, are the kinases of T118 on PNKP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from in vitro kinase assay, co-expression, and protein interaction data.

claim: WT-PNKP and T118-phosphorylated PNKP interacted with nascent DNA.
source: We found that replication fork-associated proteins, including FEN1, RPA2, and PCNA, as well as WT-PNKP and T118-phosphorylated PNKP interacted with nascent DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by iPOND assay data showing PNKP and pT118-PNKP binding to nascent DNA.

claim: The recruitment of PNKP to nascent DNA was reduced by the T118A mutation.
source: Additionally, the recruitment of PNKP to nascent DNA was reduced by the T118A mutation, which strongly suggests T118 phosphorylation is crucial for its recruitment to replication forks (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by iPOND assay data comparing WT and T118A PNKP binding to nascent DNA.

claim: Depletion of XRCC1 by siRNA treatment reduced the amount of PNKP recruited to nascent DNA.
source: Depletion of XRCC1 by siRNA treatment reduced the amount of PNKP recruited to nascent DNA, indicating the involvement of PNKP in ssDNA gap-filling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by iPOND assay data from XRCC1-depleted cells showing reduced PNKP binding to nascent DNA.

claim: Some PNKP still bound to nascent DNA after XRCC1 depletion, suggesting an alternative recruitment pathway of PNKP to DNA replication forks.
source: However, some PNKP still bound to nascent DNA, suggesting an alternative recruitment pathway of PNKP to DNA replication forks, possibly for mediating canonical OF maturation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PNKP binding to nascent DNA is reduced but not eliminated by XRCC1 depletion.

claim: CDK1/Cyclin A2 or CDK2/Cyclin A2 complex potentially regulates the phosphorylation level of PNKP T118 in the S phase, facilitating PNKP recruitment to DNA replication forks.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the CDK1/Cyclin A2 or CDK2/Cyclin A2 complex potentially regulates the phosphorylation level of PNKP T118 in the S phase, facilitating PNKP recruitment to DNA replication forks.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental results including kinase assays, cell cycle analysis, and iPOND assays.

claim: PNKP−/− and T118A-expressing cells showed increased tract length, and FEN1i treatment did not further accelerate DNA fiber length.
source: PNKP−/− and T118A-expressing cells showed increased tract length, and FEN1i treatment did not further accelerate DNA fiber length, indicating that the T118A mutation alone provokes the longer DNA tract length phenotype due to the formation of unligated OFs, similar to FEN1 inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data comparing different conditions and treatments.

claim: T118D-expressing cells exhibited normal DNA fiber tract length, similar to PNKP WT-expressing cells.
source: Conversely, T118D-expressing cells exhibited normal DNA fiber tract length, similar to PNKP WT-expressing cells, and FEN1i treatment increased DNA fiber tract length in T118D-expressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data showing normal tract length in T118D-expressing cells.

claim: T118 phosphorylation plays an essential role in proper OFs maturation akin to FEN1.
source: This suggests that the T118 phosphorylation plays an essential role in proper OFs maturation akin to FEN1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that T118A mutation phenocopies FEN1 inhibition.

claim: T118A-expressing cells in the S phase showed higher ADP-ribose intensity (1.61-fold increase vs. WT-expressing cells).
source: T118A-expressing cells in the S phase showed higher ADP-ribose intensity (1.61-fold increase vs. WT-expressing cells), similar to PNKP−/− cells (2-fold increase vs. U2OS WT cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data quantifying intensity in S phase cells.

claim: WT PNKP expression rescued the increased ADP-ribose intensity effect in PNKP−/− cells.
source: WT PNKP expression rescued this effect, suggesting that PNKP function and T118 phosphorylation are required for ssDNA gap-less DNA replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data showing rescue by WT PNKP expression.

claim: PNKP−/− cells and PNKP T118A cells showed higher ADP-ribose intensity outside the S phase (1.47-fold increase vs. WT-expressing cells).
source: Of note, PNKP−/− cells and PNKP T118A cells also showed higher ADP-ribose intensity outside the S phase (1.47-fold increase vs. WT-expressing cells), indicating that PNKP and T118 may play a role in preventing SSBs formation outside the S phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data quantifying intensity in non-S phase cells.

claim: FEN1i-treated U2OS WT cells showed increased ADP-ribose intensity.
source: FEN1i-treated U2OS WT cells showed increased ADP-ribose intensity, indicating that FEN1i treatment leads to ssDNA gap formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data from FEN1i-treated cells.

claim: The increased ADP-ribose intensity phenotype in T118A-expressing cells was not observed in FEN1i-treated T118A-expressing cells.
source: The increased ADP-ribose intensity phenotype in T118A-expressing cells was not observed in FEN1i-treated T118A-expressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data showing epistatic relationship between T118A and FEN1i.

claim: T118 phosphorylation of PNKP plays a critical role in suppressing ssDNA gap formation derived from unligated OFs in an epistatic pathway with FEN1.
source: These data suggest that T118 phosphorylation of PNKP plays a critical role in suppressing ssDNA gap formation derived from unligated OFs in an epistatic pathway with FEN1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the epistatic relationship observed between T118A mutation and FEN1 inhibition.

claim: Phosphorylation of PNKP at T118 is required to prevent unligated OF-mediated post-replicative ssDNA gap formation during DNA replication.
source: In conclusion, phosphorylation of PNKP at T118 is required to prevent unligated OF-mediated post-replicative ssDNA gap formation during DNA replication.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental results showing the role of T118 phosphorylation in preventing ssDNA gaps.

claim: PNKP T118A-expressing cells exhibited reduced repair abilities against exogenous SSB and DSB induced by IR and H2O2 treatment.
source: Incidentally, as similar to PNKP−/− cells, PNKP T118A-expressing cells exhibited reduced repair abilities against exogenous SSB and DSB induced by IR and H2O2 treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation and γH2AX foci assay data from IR and H2O2-treated cells.

claim: T118A-expressing cells showed an increased frequency of micronuclei and chromosome bridges compared to WT PNKP-complemented cells.
source: Furthermore, T118A-expressing cells showed an increased frequency of micronuclei and chromosome bridges compared to WT PNKP-complemented cells even without any treatment as well as with IR or HU treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data quantifying micronuclei and chromosome bridges.

claim: Endogenously increased ssDNA gap formation due to impaired OFs maturation in PNKP−/− and T118A-expressing cells may cause genomic instability.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that endogenously increased ssDNA gap formation due to impaired OFs maturation in PNKP−/− and T118A-expressing cells may cause genomic instability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased micronuclei and chromosome bridges in these cells.

claim: PNKP T118A mutant was still capable of dephosphorylating and phosphorylating gapped DNA ends in vitro, albeit to a lesser extent than WT PNKP.
source: Intriguingly, T118A PNKP was still capable of dephosphorylating and phosphorylating gapped DNA ends in vitro, albeit to a lesser extent than WT PNKP.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data comparing WT and T118A PNKP activities.

claim: Phosphorylation of PNKP at T118 is required for its recruitment to the gapped DNA structure but not directly for its enzymatic activity.
source: These results suggest that phosphorylation of PNKP at T118 is required for its recruitment to the gapped DNA structure but not directly for its enzymatic activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that T118A retains enzymatic activity but shows reduced DNA binding.

claim: The T118A mutant showed impaired gapped DNA-binding ability.
source: The T118A mutant showed impaired gapped DNA-binding ability, whereas the WT PNKP and the T118D mutant exhibited relatively higher binding ability than the PNKP T118A mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein-DNA binding assay data comparing WT, T118A, and T118D PNKP.

claim: D171A-expressing cells showed a spontaneously increased tract length, and FEN1i treatment did not further increase the tract length.
source: Interestingly, D171A-expressing cells showed a spontaneously increased tract length, and FEN1i treatment did not further increase the tract length.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data from D171A-expressing cells with and without FEN1i treatment.

claim: K378A-expressing cells showed longer, yet statistically non-significant, tract length than WT PNKP-expressing cells (p = 0.6293).
source: K378A-expressing cells showed longer, yet statistically non-significant, tract length than WT PNKP-expressing cells (p = 0.6293), suggesting that PNKP enzymatic activities, especially those of phosphatase, are required for accurate fork progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data from K378A-expressing cells.

claim: D171A-expressing cells showed a high ADP-ribose intensity (p < 0.0001).
source: D171A-expressing cells showed a high ADP-ribose intensity (p < 0.0001), while K378A-expressing cells exhibited relatively high ADP-ribose intensity without FEN1i treatment (p = 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ADP-ribosylation assay data from D171A-expressing cells.

claim: PNKP phosphatase and kinase activities, especially those of phosphatase, play an important role in the end-processing of OFs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that PNKP phosphatase and kinase activities, especially those of phosphatase, play an important role in the end-processing of OFs, resulting in the suppression of OF-mediated post-replicative ssDNA gap formation and ensuring accurate DNA replication (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that phosphatase-dead mutant shows more severe phenotype than kinase-dead mutant.

claim: PNKP was required for the ssDNA gap-filling pathway during DNA replication.
source: In this study, we found that PNKP was required for the ssDNA gap-filling pathway during DNA replication.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings showing PNKP involvement in gap-filling pathway.

claim: Defects in PNKP induce the accumulation of single-strand gaps in OFs and genome instability.
source: Defects in PNKP induce the accumulation of single-strand gaps in OFs and genome instability.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings showing ssDNA gap accumulation and genomic instability in PNKP-deficient cells.

claim: CDKs phosphorylate PNKP on threonine 118 (T118), mainly in the S phase.
source: We also found that CDKs phosphorylate PNKP on threonine 118 (T118), mainly in the S phase, and that CDK-mediated PNKP phosphorylation allows it to be recruited to ssDNA gaps on OFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis, in vitro kinase assays, and iPOND assays.

claim: CDK-mediated PNKP phosphorylation allows it to be recruited to ssDNA gaps on OFs.
source: We also found that CDKs phosphorylate PNKP on threonine 118 (T118), mainly in the S phase, and that CDK-mediated PNKP phosphorylation allows it to be recruited to ssDNA gaps on OFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by iPOND assays showing reduced recruitment of T118A mutant to nascent DNA.

claim: PNKP enzymatic activities, especially phosphatase activity, are required for processing of the ends of single-strand gaps on OFs.
source: Moreover, PNKP enzymatic activities, especially phosphatase activity, are required for processing of the ends of single-strand gaps on OFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber and ADP-ribosylation assays using enzymatic mutants.

claim: Phosphorylation-mediated PNKP recruitment to ssDNA gaps on OFs and the end-processing activity of PNKP are critically important for preventing genome instability through appropriate regulation of DNA replication.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that phosphorylation-mediated PNKP recruitment to ssDNA gaps on OFs and the end-processing activity of PNKP are critically important for preventing genome instability through appropriate regulation of DNA replication.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of all experimental findings in the study.

claim: PNKP has enzymatic activities as 3′-phosphatase and 5′-kinase of DNA ends to promote DNA ligation and repair.
source: Polynucleotide kinase phosphatase (PNKP) has enzymatic activities as 3′-phosphatase and 5′-kinase of DNA ends to promote DNA ligation and repair.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PNKP function.

claim: Human PNKP consists of 521 amino acids, including the forkhead-associated (FHA) domain (amino acid residues 1–110) in the amino-terminal region, and phosphatase (146–337) and kinase (341–516) domains in the carboxy-terminal region, which are connected by a linker region (111–145).
source: Human PNKP consists of 521 amino acids, including the forkhead-associated (FHA) domain (amino acid residues 1–110) in the amino-terminal region, and phosphatase (146–337) and kinase (341–516) domains in the carboxy-terminal region, which are connected by a linker region (111–145).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PNKP structure.

claim: PNKP is recruited to SSBs and DSBs sites depending on its interactions via the FHA domain of PNKP with XRCC1 and XRCC4, respectively.
source: PNKP is recruited to SSBs and DSBs sites depending on its interactions via the FHA domain of PNKP with XRCC1 and XRCC4, respectively, and is involved in base excision repair (BER), SSB repair, and non-homologous end joining for DSB repair (Breslin and Caldecott, 2009; Mani et al., 2019; Mani et al., 2010; Tsukada et al., 2020; Tsukada et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of PNKP at serine 114 by ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) is required for protein stability and efficient DNA repair for cellular survival.
source: Phosphorylation of PNKP at serine 114 by ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) is required for protein stability and efficient DNA repair for cellular survival (Segal-Raz et al., 2011; Parsons et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in PNKP are associated with the human inherited disease microcephaly and seizures (MCSZ), a neurodevelopmental disease.
source: Mutations in PNKP are associated with the human inherited disease microcephaly and seizures (MCSZ), a neurodevelopmental disease (Shen et al., 2010), ataxia oculomotor apraxia 4 (AOA4) (Bras et al., 2015), and Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT2B2), a neurodegenerative disease (Pedroso et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PNKP mutations are mostly located in the phosphatase or kinase domains and attenuate the phosphatase and kinase activities.
source: These mutations are mostly located in the phosphatase or kinase domains and attenuate the phosphatase and kinase activities (Reynolds et al., 2012; Kalasova et al., 2020; Bermúdez-Guzmán et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA replication is initiated at the origin of replication in the leading strand and at short RNA-primed DNA fragments, known as OFs, in the lagging strand.
source: DNA replication is initiated at the origin of replication in the leading strand and at short RNA-primed DNA fragments, known as OFs, in the lagging strand (Leonard and Méchali, 2013; Okazaki et al., 1968).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about DNA replication and supported by citations.

claim: ssDNA gap-filling machinery is involved in OFs maturation.
source: Recent reports suggest that single-strand DNA (ssDNA) gap-filling machinery is involved in OFs maturation (Hanzlikova et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PARP1 activity is required for efficient SSBs repair and ssDNA gap-filling pathway in OFs during DNA replication.
source: PARP1 activity is required for efficient SSBs repair and ssDNA gap-filling pathway in OFs during DNA replication (Hanzlikova et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The DNA replication machinery is precisely controlled by cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which phosphorylate several replication factors to allow them to enter the S phase and promote DNA synthesis.
source: The DNA replication machinery is precisely controlled by cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which phosphorylate several replication factors to allow them to enter the S phase and promote DNA synthesis (Swaffer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cell cycle regulation and supported by citation.

claim: When replication forks stall, ataxia telangiectasia mutated and Rad3-related protein (ATR) is activated and phosphorylates CHK1 and RPA to resolve or eliminate the impediment, promoting replication fork recovery.
source: When replication forks stall, ataxia telangiectasia mutated and Rad3-related protein (ATR) is activated and phosphorylates CHK1 and RPA to resolve or eliminate the impediment, promoting replication fork recovery (Cortez et al., 2001; Zou and Elledge, 2003).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about DNA damage response and supported by citations.
